0.text: The dataset is small (579 Q&A pairs from 90 papers). While this is stated in Limitations, conclusions about decontextualization and evaluation regimes would be stronger if corroborated on an additional, diverse long-document corpus (e.g., scientific or legal). As is, external validity is uncertain.

1.text: Downstream analysis focuses on answerability classification only. Since many scientific QA deployments require grounded answer generation, it is unclear whether the weak retrieval–downstream coupling found here would hold for generation, where faithfulness depends critically on retrieved evidence. The paper gestures at this, but does not provide empirical support.

2.text: The cross-encoder reranker is described abstractly without naming the exact checkpoint, input formatting, top-k candidates reranked, or reranking depth. Similarly, the dense retriever is loosely specified as “all-MiniLM-L6-v2” but lacks index parameters, training/tuning considerations, or normalization details that can materially affect results. These omissions hinder reproducibility and may bias outcomes in favor of sparse methods under certain templates.

3.text: For ColBERT, the specific variant, maxlen/tokenization, query/document encoders, and ANN settings are not fully enumerated, yet its full-corpus result (Table 4) is the best. More detail is needed to attribute gains to late interaction rather than confounds.

4.text: Table 1 mixes “representative models” (BM25, ColBERTv2, SPLADEv3) with “Ours” and presents disparate numbers. The provenance of the non-“Ours” rows is unclear, and it is not obvious whether these were re-run under the exact same experimental protocol. This weakens the credibility of the comparison and the message about decontextualization effects across model families.

5.text: No error bars or variance estimates are provided, although retrieval metrics and F1 can vary substantially with random seeds, ANN hyperparameters, and reranking depth. The correlation analysis in Table 8 also lacks confidence intervals and details on the correlation method (Pearson/Spearman), which limits interpretability of the “weak correlation” claim.

6.text: Templates like “aggressive_title” are referenced in results (Tables 3–6) but not fully specified in Section 3.2. Without explicit formatting or examples, it is hard to reproduce why “aggressive_title” helps ColBERT in Table 4 or BM25 in Table 3.

7.text: Query construction is not discussed. In scientific QA, question reformulation and normalization can significantly impact sparse and dense retrieval. If questions were preprocessed or truncated, it should be stated.

8.text: Indexing specifics like analyzer/tokenization for BM25/TF-IDF, stemming/stopword removal, and normalization are not detailed. These can alter the magnitude of oracle gains and the severity of full-corpus degradation.

9.text: The paper’s guidance is helpful, but some statements read more general than the evidence allows. For example, “retrieval may be optional for some tasks” (Section 4.7.2) is plausible for binary answerability, but this should be qualified more carefully so it is not misapplied to tasks where grounding is essential.

10.text: Figure 1 outlines an AI-agent pipeline for paper generation, with references to GPT-5 and Claude Opus. This is not relevant to the research methodology of the audit and distracts from the scientific content. It raises avoidable questions about scope and coherence.

11.text: The paper reports the pattern (Tables 3 and 7) but stops short of a deeper lexical versus semantic matching analysis. For instance, sparse retrievers might be penalized by title drift in tight oracle settings and aided by disambiguation in large collections. A token-level or term-weight analysis would better support the narrative.

12.text: Figure 1 is orthogonal to the core technical content. Including a figure about “paper generation” instead of an architecture diagram or qualitative retrieval examples reduces clarity and could confuse readers about the contribution.

1.text: Stress tests are described qualitatively (e.g., “94% prediction consistency” and “89% correct adjustment”), but there is no table or figure that details the protocols, number of perturbed instances, or baselines included. 2.text: In Section 4.2, the method reports Precision 63.3%, Recall 61.1%, Macro F1 54.1%, Accuracy 54.6%. For a two-class setup, such P/R values alongside a macro F1 of 54.1% may be plausible if strong class imbalance or per-class F1 diverges, but the paper does not show per-class metrics to justify the gap. This needs clarification.

3.text: Table 1 mixes diverse setups (zero-shot vs. in-context) and model families without detailing the exact prompting, calibration, or data pre-processing. It is unclear whether scores are taken from prior work, re-run, or approximated; references sometimes do not directly correspond to the model variants listed (e.g., Vicuna-7B reported 63.62 macro F1 zero-shot appears unusually high for table claim verification without detailed setup). The “—” entries further obscure comparability.

4.text: The narrative in Section 4.3 claims “surpasses basic table reasoning approaches (TAPAS-large: 50.3%),” yet Table 1 lists TAPEX-large (TabFact) at 56.06 macro F1, which would surpass the proposed 54.1. The paper should reconcile these statements and standardize the comparison set.

5.text: The paper cites QUDT/OM/UCUM ontologies but does not concretely explain how units and dimensions are represented and normalized in the system. For example, how are unit families and dimensional constraints encoded? Is there a canonical unit mapping table or UCUM parser? What is the type system used to decide cross-dimension blocking? Section 3.1–3.3 stay at a descriptive level without formalizing the representation.

6.text: The “percentage vs. percentage points” handling is asserted as robust, but the paper does not present a deterministic rule set, examples, or pseudo-code to show how the system differentiates and verifies these cases in ambiguous language contexts.

7.text: Table 2 shows w/o Percentage conversion having exactly the same metrics as the full model, and Key Findings state “0.0 F1 change,” which conflicts with the strong emphasis on percent–decimal conversions earlier in the paper. If this capability is central, the dataset used for ablation should include dedicated instances to demonstrate impact. Otherwise, the strong claims about percentage handling on SciTab need to be toned down.

8.text: The “w/o Entity heuristic” variant improves F1 (+0.4). While the authors acknowledge this, they do not adjust the main system accordingly. If the heuristic degrades performance, it should be disabled, or new logic should be introduced to avoid the harm.

9.text: The ablation baseline differs from the headline number (53.7% vs. 54.1%), and the text attributes this to implementation complexity. While plausible, the paper should include a consistent experimental harness to avoid potential confounds.

10.text: Many thresholds are hard-coded (e.g., fuzzy matching 0.6–0.7, approximate matching within 2% relative error, equality tolerances, superlative confidence rules), but there is no validation protocol or development set described for selecting them. Without a stated tuning procedure, risks of test-set overfitting or arbitrary choices remain.

11.text: Confidence calibration and decision thresholds (Section 3.4) are described heuristically without quantitative calibration (e.g., reliability diagrams) or a validation procedure.

12.text: The paper emphasizes structured reasoning traces and interpretable error taxonomy (Section 4.4), but provides no concrete example trace or case study in the main text. A small, well-chosen example would make the interpretability and unit-consistency checks far more convincing.

13.text: Figure 1 depicts an AI-driven paper generation pipeline, not the UnitMath architecture, error taxonomy, or reasoning cascade. This is off-topic for ACL and distracts from the method. 0.text: The study evaluates a single participant (Participant A) with 42 questions (Section 3.2). There is no second expert, no cross-expert transfer, and no test of whether twins capture intra-person variability. This greatly limits inferential strength for “digital twin” fidelity in strategic reasoning.

1.text: The primary metric treats option agreement as accuracy (Section 3.5). This is closer to preference classification than strategic reasoning assessment. Without validated rubrics on reasoning quality, internal consistency, or counterfactual robustness, the link to “strategic reasoning” remains weak.

2.text: Appendix A.4 states TF-IDF + cosine, but Table 2 reports three columns labeled “GPT-4o (Semantic)”, “GPT-5 (Semantic)”, and “GPT-5Pro (Semantic)”. It is unclear how these model-labeled columns arise if the method is purely TF-IDF/cosine. This inconsistency undermines interpretability.

3.text: TF-IDF cosine is largely lexical and not fit for capturing structural reasoning alignment. Contemporary embedding-based or entailment-based metrics, or rubric-based human+LLM adjudication with reliability checks, would be more appropriate. No inter-annotator agreement or human rating protocol is reported.

4.text: There is no trivial baseline such as majority-choice, random-choice, or a “generic model with no persona and no RAG.” Without these, it is hard to know whether the reported ~50% is actually strong, marginal, or within reach of chance or simple heuristics, especially on multi-option questions.

5.text: No ablation disentangles how much persona prompting versus RAG contributes to the gains. Given the paper’s focus on “digital twin,” this is essential.

6.text: No confidence intervals, no bootstrapping across items, and no run-to-run variance with different decoding seeds (even though the models are stochastic). Section “Experiment statistical significance” in the checklist itself acknowledges the absence of error bars. This leaves unclear whether the small spreads in Table 1 are meaningful.

7.text: While Figures 3–4 show screenshots of custom GPTs and Appendix A.1 contains sketch text, the exact persona/RAG prompts, retrieval settings, chunking, and re-ranking details needed to interpret and replicate the pipeline are only partially described. The paper states verification questions were withheld from RAG, but the construction of the KB, exclusion filters, and retrieval diagnostics are not quantified.

8.text: The paper attributes higher semantic similarity for certain Chinese LLMs (Table 2, Table 3) to cultural proximity. There is no pre-registered hypothesis test, no language-controlled re-runs, no bilingual prompting conditions, and no human judgment study to validate this explanation. As presented, it is a post-hoc narrative.

9.text: The 42 verification questions mix binary policy stances with bundled trade-offs (Appendix A.3) but we do not see evidence that these items underwent psychometric validation (difficulty, discrimination, test-retest stability) or that they cleanly isolate participant-specific reasoning features rather than general leadership heuristics learned by LLMs.

10.text: Section 3.6–3.7 describes AI-led analysis, drafting, and self-assessment by custom reviewer agents (Appendix A.2). While innovative, relying on the same or closely related model family to produce and to evaluate the narrative risks shared failure modes or bias. No human cross-check of key statistics or an independent human evaluator study is provided.

11.text: Figure 1: The quadrant labeling suggests actionable “top-right” models for deployment, yet the underlying differences are small and lack uncertainty bounds. The plot is visually persuasive but may overstate separability without significance testing.

12.text: Figure 2: Per-difficulty bars make the decay trend clear, but no per-item counts or difficulty calibration are provided. Without knowing how many items per level and whether levels are balanced across topics, comparisons may be brittle.

0.text: The core experiments rely on “GPT-5,” “o3,” and “o4-mini” (Section 4.1) without specifying public availability, versions, or API configurations. No seeds, prompts, or raw review outputs are provided in the main paper. As a result, reproducing the exact acceptance rates and concern metrics seems infeasible from the current description alone. This is especially problematic because all results hinge on behaviors of particular model variants and prompts.

1.text: The number of seeds and total number of generated papers is under-specified. Section 4.1 says “Each seed produces 4 papers across six strategy setups,” but does not report the number of seeds. Without an explicit N for each condition, the statistical credibility of Table 1, Table 2, and Figure 1 is hard to assess.

2.text: Integrity Concern Rate (ICR) is computed via c_m(x) = Γ(ω_m(x)) where Γ is a GPT-5 judge (Section 4.1–4.2). There is no human-audited validation set or inter-annotator agreement to establish precision/recall of Γ. If Γ is misclassifying generic caveats as “integrity concerns,” ICRs and the downstream “conflict” metric in Table 2 can be materially distorted.

3.text: The method conflates “AI-generated text” detection with “scientific fabrication/integrity” detection in the mitigation design. ReD and DetOnly explicitly task the models with detecting whether content is AI-generated, not whether claims or evidence are fabricated (Section 5.1). This target mismatch likely explains some poor detection performance in Table 4 and weak coupling to acceptance in Table 3; it also reduces the relevance of those mitigation results to the central research question.

4.text: Section 3.4 gives a careful stratified calibration procedure, but Section 4.1 provides only N_cal=200 and the final thresholds (τ_rate=7, τ_0.5=6.667). There is no analysis of calibration goodness (e.g., reliability diagrams, confidence intervals for π(t), or sensitivity of thresholds to bin choices), which would help justify that thresholds faithfully mirror venue decisions. It is also unclear how reviewer rubrics map to a single scalar s(x) beyond “take the overall assessment.” If the underlying models differ in rubric semantics, this scalarization may not be consistent across models.

5.text: The paper states that the generator “allows the LLM to freely generate any necessary experimental results and plotting code” (Section 4.1) and samples pseudo-data D ∼ q(·|s, t, θ) (Equation 2), but does not document q, priors over effect sizes, or visual artifact templates. How were the fake results constrained to be “plausible”? Without a description of generation distributions, it is impossible to reason about how easily a normal reviewer should have caught anomalies.

6.text: The “ProofGap” strategy claims to include a theorem with a hidden oversight (Section 3.2), yet the paper provides no example theorem, lemma, or proof sketch that would allow readers to assess how challenging the oversight is to detect. This weakens the internal validity of S5-related claims.

7.text: Table 1, Table 2, and Table 3 report percentages without Ns or confidence intervals. Figure 1 histograms also omit sample counts. Without basic uncertainty quantification, the magnitude of reported effects is hard to assess statistically.

8.text: The results section (Section 4.2) interprets model behavior qualitatively but does not report statistical tests (e.g., bootstrap CIs) to check whether differences between strategies or models are significant.

9.text: Table 2 computes conflict “within papers where the model raised a concern” as the share still getting an acceptance-level score. However, concerns in reviews often coexist with positive decisions when issues are non-fatal. The authors assert that this is a “fundamental breakdown,” but do not analyze whether the flagged concerns are truly integrity-critical (e.g., fabricated results) versus stylistic/clarity issues. Given that Γ controls labeling and is not validated, over-interpretation is a risk.

10.text: Figure 1 is central to the paper’s claims. It shows consistent right shifts for o4-mini and fatter right tails for o3 across S1–S5 and ALL. However, the figure caption and text (Page 6) do not disclose the per-setup sample sizes or whether bins/axes were standardized across strategies. Without Ns, it is impossible to judge whether the observed differences are robust or a sampling artifact.

11.text: Table 4 evaluates detectors on a 100-paper mixed set (Section 5.2), but the class balance and exact composition per strategy are not fully detailed beyond “50 real, 50 generated.” Since detectors are asked to label AI-generated content rather than fabricated claims, the near-chance results are difficult to interpret as evidence about detecting scientific fabrication.

12.text: The checklist answers “[Yes]” to “complete and correct proofs” and points to Section 3, yet the main paper contains no theorems or formal proofs. This inconsistency undermines confidence in other checklist items and suggests the paper may have unchecked boilerplate.

13.text: The evaluation is bound to a single venue/year and three specific models with one fixed rubric. No cross-venue, cross-rubric, or cross-family sensitivity analysis is presented. Conclusions such as “fabricated papers achieve acceptance rates up to 82%” may not hold under modest changes in models, prompts, or calibration. Some tempering in the claims is warranted.

14.text: While the paper cites several relevant studies, recent work that directly benchmarks LLM reviewers, prompt-injection defenses, and review-detection pipelines is not discussed (see “Potentially Missing Related Work” below). These omissions limit the paper’s positioning and the interpretive lens for its results.

15.text: Figure 1: The reported right shift for o4-mini and heavy right tail for o3 are consistent with the paper’s narrative that o4-mini is the most accepting and o3 exhibits greater variance. However, the absence of Ns and CIs makes it hard to gauge whether S1’s rightward shift is statistically reliable or driven by a small sample. Please add exact counts per bar and confidence intervals.

16.text: Table 1: S1’s ACPT 67.0%/82.0% is central to the paper’s most striking claim. This table needs Ns per row and per model, plus uncertainty estimates. Also clarify whether ACPT uses only the consensus scalar or per-model scores.

17.text: Table 2: Concern–acceptance conflict rates are compelling, especially the 100% entries for o4-mini in S1/S3/All. But without understanding the severity/type of concerns that Γ labeled, it is not clear that these rows indicate integrity failure rather than a reviewer accepting with minor concerns.

18.text: Table 3: ReD increases both ICR@M and acceptance rates. This is an important and counterintuitive result; however, it could also be an artifact of concurrent prompting that asks the same model to do two tasks with mismatched targets. Ablate the prompt to decouple the review score from the detection subtask, or gate acceptance on explicit risk tiers, and then re-report ACPT by risk tier.

19.text: Table 4: Since ReD and DetOnly are asked to detect AI-generated text rather than fabrication, the interpretation should be reframed as “how well can we triage AI-generated text?” rather than “can we detect fabrication?” Consider an additional detector targeting internal statistical consistency, baseline sanity checks, or provenance.

0.text: Section 5.1 claims replication of the “third-quarter phenomenon,” but provides only qualitative alignment from plots (Figure 3), without formal statistical detection tests (e.g., changepoint analysis or planned contrasts on third-quarter windows) or quantitative effect-size comparisons to published mission trajectories. The absence of raw analog data is understandable, but then the validation claim should be framed as face validity, not strong external validity.

1.text: Coping-strategy labels in Table 2 (Emotion-Focused vs Problem-Focused vs Avoidance) appear to be produced by LLM-based classification (Section 4 mentions “classifying dialogue”), yet no annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement against human coders, or error analysis is provided. As a result, model “behavioral fingerprints” may be artifacts of the labeler model.

2.text: The same class of models generates behaviors and also performs reflective updates (Equation 1 via f_LLM) and sometimes evaluates effectiveness (PSA “dynamic effectiveness check,” Section 3.3). This introduces a closed-loop bias: the judge shares priors and style with the generator. The PSA itself is always powered by GPT-4.1-mini (Section 4), which may advantage GPT-family agents in both communication style and judged effectiveness. These design choices undermine claims of causal impact and fair cross-model comparisons.

3.text: Section 5.2 and Table 1 repeatedly describe PSA effects as “causal.” Within-simulation A/B toggles of an intervention and permutation tests support internal contrasts, but they do not establish causal claims about real crews or even generally about LLM-driven social systems, given the endogenous LLM evaluation loop. The PSA’s “success” is also partly determined by another LLM, which conflates treatment and measurement.

4.text: Only 10 iterations per condition (Section 4) seem low for high-variance agentic simulations; CIs and permutation p-values may be sensitive to a few outliers. Bootstrapping on such small n helps but does not fully mitigate.

5.text: “Persistent crew” profiles are generated once by GPT-4.1-mini and reused across all model conditions (Section 4). This risks biasing language style, interaction norms, and persona fit toward GPT-4.1, which could differentially benefit the GPT series in Tables 1–2 and Figure 3. An alternative is to regenerate matched crews per base model or to randomize crew seeds and report stratified or mixed-effects analyses.

6.text: Cohesion is defined as inverse standard deviation (Equation 3). This is unbounded above and dominated by small denominators; it also collapses to infinity as variance approaches zero. Reporting standard deviation directly, or a bounded transformation (e.g., 1 / (1 + σ)) would be more stable. Sensitivity analyses are missing.

7.text: Psychological Keystone Index uses the maximum rolling correlation (Equation 4). Taking a max across windows inflates scores and invites selection bias; reporting mean or percentile-based summaries, and significance testing against null permutations of time-series, would be more defensible.

8.text: The reflective update function f_LLM (Equations 1–2) is central, but no evidence is given that its outputs track human stress or loneliness changes. Appendix A.1 constrains deltas between −0.1 and 0.1, but there is no calibration or validation against human annotations or empirical data (e.g., longitudinal diaries, physiological proxies). Without such grounding, the time-series in Figures 3–4 may reflect prompt priors rather than credible psychosocial trajectories.

9.text: Table 1 and Table 4 show stress reductions, but the PSA’s decision policy (Appendix A.3) and intervention content (Appendix A.4) are not externally evaluated. The “effectiveness check” after interventions is rendered by “another LLM call” (Section 3.3) rather than human raters or predefined success criteria. This risks confirmation bias.

10.text: The PSA is active on all days with the same model and thresholding; ablations such as randomized or placebo messages, rate-limited PSA, or a scripted CBT baseline would better isolate mechanisms.

11.text: No comparison to a non-LLM agent-based model that uses simple stress-update heuristics; such a baseline would test whether the claimed phenomena require LLM agents or arise from the event schedule and aggregation alone.

12.text: No human-in-the-loop qualitative assessment of dialogue realism beyond sentiment-and-coping tags. Incorporating a small human rating study on a sample of crisis dialogues (e.g., Figure 1b) would strengthen claims that agents behave “in character” under stress.

13.text: Multiple-comparison control is not discussed, yet many model-mission-condition contrasts are tested (Tables 1 and 4). Some p-values are marginal (e.g., 0.0211 for Mixed in HI-SEAS IV) and could flip under FDR correction. The paper also sometimes emphasizes percentage reductions without standardized effect sizes.

14.text: For the claimed third-quarter pattern, the paper does not specify pre-registered time windows, leading to post-hoc interpretation of Figure 3 trends.

15.text: The paper proposes PsySpace as a benchmark for “social intelligence of generative agents” (Abstract, Section 6), but metrics are domain-specific and partially self-labeled. Clearer articulation of what general capability is being benchmarked and how to reuse the suite outside space missions would help.

16.text: Figure 1: The pre- vs post-crisis bar plots illustrate shifts in individual stress, but there is no y-axis labeling detail in the main text and it is unclear how large these deltas are relative to daily variance. This weakens the point about “individual psychological responses” unless quantified.

17.text: Figures 3 and 4: The plots are persuasive for visual inspection, but the manuscript relies on them to assert the third-quarter effect (e.g., 3a and 3b). A formal test would make those claims more convincing.

18.text: Table 2: It reports “Dominant Coping Strategy” per model. The method for aggregating per-event labels, resolving ties, and controlling for event mix is not specified, leaving open whether differences reflect labeling bias or true behavioral tendencies.

19.text: Xygkou-Tsiamoulou et al., “COSMIC: Emotionally Intelligent Agents to Support Mental and Emotional Well-being in Extreme Isolation: Lessons from Analog Astronaut Training Missions,” 2026 — Field deployment of emotionally intelligent AI support in analog missions; directly comparable to the PSA. This is crucial, because, per Section 3.6, the LLM does not perform inference or optimization but “interprets” externally computed scores. Without comparing to a non-LLM selector, it is unclear whether the LLM contributes to decision quality beyond reporting the argmax. This unaddressed baseline directly impacts claims of LLM-plus-ID superiority.

1.text: Table 1 (main text) reports very strong alignment (97.5%) and ΔEU near zero; Appendix Table 2 (observed-only recomputation) reports markedly lower alignment for Mentor-Mind (0.8951) and shows different ΔEU patterns. While the paper explains the private vs. public oracle differences, the divergence is large enough to cast doubt on headline claims. The text should reconcile these discrepancies more rigorously, quantifying how private thresholds and policies shift the metrics and why readers should trust Table 1 as the “official” view. As it stands, this undermines the reliability of the reported effect sizes.

2.text: The paper uses λ for mean–CVaR trade-off in Section 3.4, but Section 4.3 discusses “β” for risk settings, which is not previously defined. This is a small but important clarity issue. Given the core contribution is risk-aware decision-making, inconsistent notation makes it harder to reason about ablations and replicate settings.

3.text: In Section 4.3 and Tables 3–4, after post-hoc repair (HCVR neutralized) the feasible-only ΔEU gaps across methods become small and can even reduce Mentor-Mind’s advantage. The narrative still states Mentor-Mind “retains the best feasible-only ΔEU,” but the values in Tables 3–4 are very close and sometimes suggest minimal separation. The paper should quantify statistical significance on the feasible-only ΔEU and characterize where and why the ID scaffold still helps, or temper the claim.

4.text: Section 4.2 mentions CoT+Simulator as future work. This is essential for a fair comparison, since Mentor-Mind’s gains plausibly come from simulator access and hard-filtering, not from the ID per se. 0.text: The paper is a materials discovery study using LLMs; it does not address language modeling research, NLP tasks, datasets, evaluation, or theory. While it leverages a text interface and retrieval, the contribution is to catalyst design, not NLP. This alone warrants desk rejection for ACL.

1.text: The second-stage filter uses “overpotential < 500 mV” for retrieved entries. Materials Project and NOMAD generally do not include OER overpotentials; OC20 provides surface–adsorbate energetics but not OER overpotential records ready for that filter. The paper does not explain how overpotentials for the database items were obtained or standardized across sources, which undermines the validity of the retrieval criterion and any claims dependent on it.

2.text: The caption of Table 1 states “Wilcoxon signed‑rank test with Bonferroni correction (α=0.0002 for 250 comparisons).” Signed‑rank tests require paired measurements; it is unclear what the pairing is across heterogeneous catalysts. Similarly, Section 3.5 cites bootstrap CIs, Wilcoxon tests, and paired t‑tests without precise definitions of the paired structure, the compared distributions, or the multiple-comparison design. These issues cast doubt on the reported significance statements.

3.text: The prompt encodes a cost ceiling of $5,000/kg and “<30% precious metal content.” Yet the top‑activity entry in Table 1 has a listed cost of $27,000/kg and 40% Ir+Ru (0.1+0.3), and the second row includes 15% Pt with $4,500/kg total cost but still precious metal content above or near the ceiling elsewhere. The paper needs to reconcile how such candidates pass the constraint-based filtering and why the ceiling appears ignored in practice.

4.text: The paper reports 4,200 CPU‑hours vs 840,000 for 10^6 compositions. However, the work also states full OER energetics and stability checks were computed for 250+ candidates with slab models, which typically require significant sampling. No wall‑clock breakdown is provided for surface relaxations, intermediate energies, and ensemble DFTs mentioned for error bars. Without a transparent accounting, the 200× claim reads optimistic.

5.text: Figure 2 and Figure 5 use “mixing enthalpy” and ΔE_NOH as core axes, yet the main text does not rigorously define their computation for multi‑component HEAs on surfaces vs bulk phases. 0.text: The core promise is “language-native” multi-agent interaction, yet the paper does not specify whether agents meaningfully converse with one another or only emit independent action–intention pairs each round. Section 2.6 and the Method Box detail returns (w, FTE, p + intention) and constraints, but do not describe message passing, negotiation protocols, memory, or coordination beyond shared rules. Without explicit interaction mechanics, it is unclear how this differs from parallel single-agent decision stubs with shared exogenous shocks. This undermines the “social” part of social simulation and limits interpretability of emergent dynamics.

1.text: Critical implementation details are missing from the main text. The paper does not specify the prompting schema, role instructions, decoding parameters (temperature, nucleus sampling), or how randomness is controlled beyond “fixed seeds.” Since the results hinge on LLM behavior and its stochasticity, these details are necessary for ACL-level reproducibility and for interpreting sensitivity. The “Reproducibility Statement” promises an anonymized artifact, but the main paper should still document key hyperparameters and decision rules.

2.text: The DID analysis claims agent-clustered SEs and time fixed effects, but the paper does not report: Pre-trend checks or an event-study plot to assess parallel trends, which is central to DID validity. Placebo or staggered-window checks to ensure the effect is not driven by early shocks or drift. Sensitivity to alternative specifications (e.g., random effects, block bootstrap, aggregating to group-level panels).

3.text: Figure 1 shows post-policy DID bars with CIs, but without pre-period dynamics it is difficult to assess whether the near-zero employment effects are a reliable consequence or an artifact of design.

4.text: The design uses 20 agents per group with NJ:PA = 16:4 (Method Box). This is an unusual and highly imbalanced “treatment-control” composition that risks unstable DID estimates, especially for employment where variance is large. The authors should justify this ratio, report power analyses or at least precision metrics, and clarify whether results are robust to alternative NJ:PA mixes. Table 2’s employment DID shows very large swings (e.g., C: −28.9 FTE) that suggest instability.

5.text: The paper repeatedly claims employment effects are “≈0” or “statistically indistinguishable from zero,” yet the right panel of Figure 1 shows wide CIs around employment DID estimates for A/B/C/D. Without numeric CIs or p-values, it is hard to substantiate the “≈0” framing. Table 2’s employment DIDs vary in sign and magnitude across runs, further suggesting high variance that needs deeper analysis (e.g., distributional summaries across all weeks and agents, not only a single DID point).

6.text: Section 3.2 presents a few representative intentions, but does not analyze them systematically. If intention texts are a key differentiator of MASS, the paper should code them with a transparent scheme, report inter-annotator agreement, and link intention distributions to numeric outcomes. As written, the mechanism story is anecdotal and concentrated in the single run where intentions were required (D), which introduces reporting bias relative to A/B/C.

7.text: The paper positions MASS as a “low-risk platform for ex-ante policy probing and extreme counterfactuals.” Given the limited interaction modeling, lack of pre-trend diagnostics, high employment variance, and small sample size, the validation is not strong enough to generalize the framework’s reliability for policy-relevant ex-ante evaluation. Stronger evidence is needed across diverse policy domains and model variants.

8.text: There are no comparisons to standard ABM baselines or to alternative LLM-agent frameworks under the same scenario. Nor are there ablations showing the effect of key design choices: with vs. without intention texts, with different decoding temperatures, with/without legal price bands, or with different time granularities. These are essential to isolate what in MASS is responsible for the observed effects.

9.text: The “AI Agent Setup” cites GPT-5 series, with no cross-model checks. Given that behavioral outputs can vary substantially across foundation models, at least one alternative model replication is warranted. Otherwise, generality is not demonstrated.

10.text: Figure 1 does not include numeric CIs, making it hard to verify the “≈0” employment conclusion. Table 2 reports only point estimates for four runs, and omits standard errors or CIs. The paper also lacks an event-study figure to demonstrate pre-trends, and does not provide a distributional figure for intention categories, which would directly serve the mechanism-audit claim.

11.text: Without clear interaction mechanisms and diagnostics, the central claim that language-native multi-agent simulation yields credible social-process evidence is undercut. The DID claims for employment, the most contentious outcome, are not sufficiently supported by the uncertainty quantification shown in Figure 1 and the volatility seen in Table 2. Missing baselines/ablations and single-model dependency limit the methodological insight and broader reproducibility. Overall, the idea is promising but the empirical and methodological validation needs to be strengthened to meet main-track standards.

12.text: Figure 1: Wage DID bars support the wage-lift claim; employment DID CIs appear wide, raising doubts about the “≈0” effect characterization without numeric intervals.

13.text: Table 2: Wage DID magnitudes are consistent across A/B/D, but employment DID shows large magnitudes and sign variation, suggesting instability and the need for pre-trend checks and precision reporting.

14.text: Equation (1): The anchoring argument is plausible, but it does not substitute for missing details on interaction protocols and agent communication needed to justify “social” emergence.

0.text: Table 1 reports only recall on a restricted set of 20 drugs and omits precision and F1. Without precision, the practical value of 640 extracted associations cannot be assessed. High false‑positive rates would invalidate downstream novelty flags and hypothesis generation.

1.text: The recall computation is unconventional: matching to the “top‑5 highest frequency adverse effects per drug in FAERS” is a coarse and biased ground truth. This penalizes quality‑of‑life ADRs that are less represented in FAERS and privileges severe outcomes like “death,” confounding the interpretation of the reported 0.08–0.27 recall.

2.text: No human‑labeled evaluation set is provided. There is no inter‑annotator agreement, error taxonomy, or qualitative error analysis of extraction failures.

3.text: The paper does not specify normalization of Reddit colloquialisms to MedDRA or SNOMED terms. Consequently, both Table 1’s evaluation and Table 2’s “novel” associations may be artifacts of vocabulary mismatch (e.g., “daytime sleepiness” vs. “somnolence,” “bloating” vs. “abdominal distension”). This undermines the Verifier’s zero‑count findings.

4.text: Equation‑level clarity is missing: the Verifier score is defined as ln(FAERS_count + 1), but mapping rules that connect Reddit expressions to FAERS PTs are unspecified, so the score is not interpretable across pairs.

5.text: Temporal, confidence, and community scores are described qualitatively on Page 2, but specific extraction rules, prompts, thresholds, or calibration procedures are not given. There is no validation that these scores correlate with ground‑truth temporality or reporter certainty.

6.text: Community support uses upvotes and replies, but the paper does not report how these raw counts were normalized across subreddits or time, nor does it show that “engagement” correlates with signal quality. Confounding popularity with validity is a risk not addressed empirically.

7.text: Table 3 lists confounders (e.g., “male,” “recent surgery,” “multiple myeloma”), yet the paper does not detail how the Analyzer extracts, aggregates, and ranks confounders from text, nor how it distinguishes confounders from mediators or colliders. No manual audit is presented to evaluate correctness. Without causal framing or validation, these outputs risk misleading interpretations.

8.text: Table 2 flags five associations with zero FAERS counts as “potentially novel,” but the pipeline does not include synonym expansion, multi‑level aggregation (e.g., HLT/HLGT in MedDRA), or check for label wording variants. Several listed ADRs plausibly exist under related PTs. Without a robust normalization layer and literature triangulation protocol, “novelty” is not substantiated.

9.text: Only 187 Reddit posts are analyzed, yet 640 associations are reported. This ratio suggests extensive many‑to‑many extraction per post, raising concerns about over‑fragmentation or hallucinated pairings. The paper does not quantify evidence instances per association or provide per‑pair support distributions.

10.text: No temporal hold‑out or prospective simulation beyond anecdotal case studies. The pre‑2017 restriction in Section 4 is informative but remains qualitative and selective rather than a systematic early‑warning backtest.

11.text: Table 4 contains rich mechanistic narratives with citations, but there is no verification step to check citation correctness, recency, or direct relevance. In the absence of human curation or automated reference validation, there is material risk of plausible‑sounding but imprecise or off‑target mechanistic stories.

12.text: The paper cites foundational social‑media pharmacovigilance work but omits several recent, directly comparable systems that mine web forums or Reddit and connect to FAERS, knowledge graphs, and GUIs. This weakens positioning and denies readers an empirical and design‑level context.

13.text: Prompts for each agent, post‑processing rules, entity dictionaries, normalization resources, and Reddit sampling procedures are not specified in enough operational detail to ensure replication. Compute budgets and inference settings are not reported per agent. Given closed models, these details are necessary.

14.text: Figure 1: The pipeline diagram communicates flow well, but it elides crucial normalization, de‑duplication, and aggregation steps between Explorer and Verifier. The right‑hand claim “Parosmia still not formally associated with imatinib (2022)” is presented without systematic evidence or cross‑terminology search, which weakens the case study’s generality.

15.text: Figure 2: The UI mockups are helpful, but the Analyzer Report panel does not indicate term mappings, evidence counts per association, or confidence intervals for scores. Without provenance links to specific Reddit posts and their time stamps, auditability is limited.

16.text: Table 1: Reporting only “Total Drugs,” “Total Associations,” and “Recall” on a restricted set is insufficient for an IE task. A precision/recall/F1 breakdown, error categories, and per‑drug variability are needed.

17.text: Table 2: The five “top” novel associations are ranked by high Analyzer scores, but those scores are themselves unvalidated. Zero FAERS counts, when produced without synonym/ontology alignment, are not strong novelty evidence.

18.text: Table 3: The notion of “saliency” for confounders is defined as the number of unique symptoms they touch. This ignores prevalence, effect size, and causal plausibility; a frequency‑only criterion risks over‑calling generic descriptors.

19.text: Table 4: The Proposer’s outputs read like well‑formed literature‑based narratives. Absent a verification step or expert adjudication, they should be framed as speculative; the paper occasionally implies higher confidence than warranted.

0.text: The core evidence comes from three AI-simulated students in AI self-play on one for-loop problem. Without real learners, learning measures, or multiple tasks, it is unclear whether the observed metacognitive or conceptual gains would manifest in practice. This is acknowledged in Section 6 but it substantially limits the paper’s contribution for an ACL venue focused on empirically grounded NLP/AI-in-education advances.

1.text: Methods (Page 4) note running all three personas in one GPT-4o chat session. Even with restated headers and phase resets, cross-persona carryover and demand characteristics are credible threats to internal validity. Results may reflect tutor memory or stylistic momentum more than persona-specific learning dynamics.

2.text: The paper explicitly avoids formal coding and does not report counts or intercoder agreement. As a result, the claims about “recurrent misconceptions” and “metacognitive moves” rest on close reading alone. For ACL standards, even qualitative studies usually provide an explicit codebook, unit of analysis, and basic reliability or triangulation.

3.text: The seven-phase protocol is proposed post hoc, but there are no ablations checking whether Slow Thinking, Incremental Probing, or Transfer independently add value. This prevents isolating which parts of the protocol actually drive the observed effects.

4.text: The GPT-3.5 “with vs. without protocol” contrast (Section 5.1) illustrates dynamics but remains qualitative and subjective, lacking standardized measures or coding. Moreover, the main simulations used GPT-4o, while the baseline contrast uses GPT-3.5; the paper is careful not to draw cross-model inferences, but this choice still complicates readers’ interpretation of protocol-driven vs. model-driven effects.

5.text: Although Human-Centered NLP and Dialogue Systems are within scope, the study’s evidence is descriptive and rests on simulated data. Without objective measures, comparative baselines involving human tutors or alternative dialogue strategies, or even simple quantitative indicators (e.g., counts of self-corrections), the contribution feels premature for ACL main track.

6.text: Figure 1 (Page 5) is a phase summary table with brief log excerpts. It is helpful for understanding the design but is not evidence of learning or metacognition.

7.text: Figure 2 (Page 7) presents a “within-model qualitative contrast” table for five dimensions. It is essentially a claim summary, not a result grounded in coded observations. To support these five dimensions convincingly, the paper needs a minimal analytic tally or rubric applied consistently across transcripts.

8.text: The Transfer phase is highlighted as a main refinement, but it is not evaluated on new problems or datasets in the main (GPT-4o) simulations. Claims that it promotes generalization are plausible but untested in this work.

9.text: While prompts and logs are released, outcomes with proprietary models can vary with updates and sampling parameters. The paper states default UI settings were used, but no seeds or settings were controlled. This makes replication possible only in a loose, qualitative sense.

10.text: The paper spans time references such as “May–Sep 2025” sessions and later 2025–2026 citations; while not necessarily incorrect, it further underscores that results may hinge on specific model states and UIs at particular times.

11.text: The baseline states “free, not logged,” which hampers auditability and exact replication.

12.text: Figure 1 (Page 5): Positively, this tabular figure clarifies phase intentions with concrete log snippets, making the protocol understandable at a glance. However, as evidence it is purely descriptive; the paper would be stronger if Figure 1 were complemented by a result table that quantitatively summarizes, for example, the number of self-correction events or clarification prompts per phase across the three transcripts.

13.text: Figure 2 (Page 7): The comparison table claims consistent differences across “interaction structure,” “student role,” “error handling,” “metacognition,” and “dialogic learning” for GPT‑3.5 with vs. without protocol. Since these are the core claims of added value, they need to be supported by a results table that reports minimal counts or coded instances drawn from Appendix D logs (e.g., number of diagnostic questions, student-initiated refinements, or metacognitive statements). Without that, Figure 2 reads as an interpretive summary rather than substantiated findings.

14.text: Without minimal measurement, baselines, or ablations, readers cannot assess whether the observed improvements are robust to prompt phrasing, model variance, or simple tutoring heuristics. The lack of real learners and coding prevents the work from informing design practice beyond anecdotal guidance.

0.text: The experimental section is extremely lean for an empirical systems paper. Table 1 is the sole quantitative results table. There are no error bars, confidence intervals, or seed-controlled replications reported in the main paper, despite the complexity and stochasticity of LLM-based systems. The Agents4Science checklist statement that “replicated runs across randomized initializations/topologies” were reported is not reflected with concrete statistics in the main text; the Results section does not present variability measures. This makes it difficult to assess the robustness of the throughput and pass-rate differences.

1.text: The study scope is small: three task families with similar trends but without deeper breakdowns (e.g., per-agent output distributions, time-series of test pass rates, composition depth trajectories per round). The claims about balanced contributions and “lower top share” in Section 4.2 are not substantiated with explicit numeric evidence in the main text.

2.text: The evolutionary selection is driven by average TCI (Section 3.3), which explicitly does not weight correctness or collaboration metrics (“selection is TCI-based without directly weighting correctness or collaboration metrics,” Page 5). This can reward tool bloat or superficial interface breadth rather than utility or reliability. Although a parsing quality gate penalizes syntax errors (Section 4.1), the evolutionary objective does not directly consider pass rates or real downstream task value. This weakens the causal link between selection pressure and the desirable emergent properties the paper aims to study.

3.text: As corroborated in Table 1, the “Compositional complexity” column under Boids is near zero across domains (0.03/0.04/0.01), which suggests the TCI’s composition component is not being effectively selected for in practice, undercutting the intended “evolution toward reusable parts.”

4.text: The paper itself acknowledges potential confounds (Page 7: “per-round build enforcement and ‘novelty-seeking’ cues” may drive the observed gains), but no ablations are presented to separate the effects of (i) Boids prompts versus (ii) deterministic build enforcement versus (iii) evolutionary selection. For instance, a “build-enforcement only” condition, or an “evolution only” condition with correctness-weighted selection, would be valuable. Section 3.3 says the authors study “boids-only, evolution-only, and combined conditions,” yet the reported results only contrast “Baseline (Global) vs Boids+Evolution” in Table 1; there is no table or figure showing boids-only or evolution-only outcomes.

5.text: The core claim is about emergent coordination and ecosystem dynamics. However, the only quantitative evidence is overall throughput and pass rates. There are no quantitative measurements of collaboration events, adoption graphs, or specialization indices, despite these being identified as observables in Section 3.1. Qualitative examples of cross-agent reuse, or dependency graphs illustrating how cohesion/alignment influenced tool chaining, are absent.

6.text: The cohesion rule (Equation 6) is intended to favor using neighbors’ tools, but Table 1 shows reduced compositional complexity under Boids+Evolution. This contradiction should be explicitly analyzed: why does the cohesion prompt fail to raise composition scores in practice? Is it outweighed by separation, by the deterministic “build” step, by dependency policy limits, or by the TCI incentives?

7.text: TCI is a static, non-semantic proxy (Section 5.2). Particularly, Ccomp weights breadth over depth and counts top-level imports and tool references. This can be gamed by superficial wrapper code and does not reflect actual runtime reuse or utility. Given that a central claim is about composition and emergent pipelines, the lack of dynamic call-graph or runtime composition metrics is a significant gap. The paper acknowledges this but still bases selection entirely on TCI.

8.text: The discrepancy between the narrative and Table 1’s “Compos. complexity” highlights potential construct-validity issues: the system is said to “encourage composition,” yet the measured indicator shows composition falling near zero.

9.text: The “Baseline (Global)” is not fully specified in the main text beyond high-level descriptions. Key elements are missing: Are prompts identical except for Boids fragments? Is the per-round deterministic build enforcement used in baseline? How are examples/exemplars surfaced to baseline agents? Without a rigorously controlled baseline, improvements in “Tools created” could reflect differences in prompting template complexity and variety rather than inherent benefits of local-rule conditioning.

10.text: Table 1’s “Pass rate (%)” is ambiguous: are these pass rates per-submission, per-tool, or per-final-promoted tool? Are multiple retries allowed? The Discussion mentions “lightweight, failure-aware retries” as a possible extension, but it is unclear what retry protocol, if any, was in place during reported runs.

11.text: While tool creation with LLM agents is relevant to ACL, the current tasks and metrics are not strongly tied to standard NLP evaluation practices. The paper would be much stronger if it connected to recognized NLP agent/tool benchmarks, or at least to text-heavy evaluation suites where composition depth can be objectively correlated with downstream performance (e.g., complex IE or multi-hop QA with tool calls).

12.text: The text-analysis domain is mentioned, but the empirical analysis remains framework-centric. There is no direct comparison to multi-agent orchestration baselines common in NLP (e.g., CAMEL/AutoGen-style pipelines executing text-processing workflows with tool reuse).

13.text: There are no figures visualizing tool ecosystems, adoption graphs, specialization divergence, or composition depth over time. This is a missed opportunity to demonstrate the paper’s central thesis about emergent organization. Even a single figure showing evolving dependency graphs per round would materially strengthen the narrative.

14.text: Section 4.2 asserts “the gain is ecosystem-wide rather than star-driven: the most productive agent accounts for a smaller share of total output,” but no data are provided to back this. A simple Lorenz curve or top-k share table would suffice.

15.text: The Conclusions state “30–50% more valid artifacts than global baselines,” which is roughly consistent with Table 1 tool counts, but “valid” implies test-passing artifacts; the paper should directly report “number of passing tools” per regime to substantiate this term.

16.text: The Acknowledgements specify Azure OpenAI endpoints and a single deployment “gpt-4.1-nano,” but there are no details on random seeds, rate limiting, retry/backoff policies, or cost/accounting. Given the stochasticity of LLM sampling, reproducibility requires more than endpoint details. The paper mentions logs/JSON emission but does not provide a concrete protocol in the main text for reconstructing Table 1 from these artifacts.

17.text: Equation (6) (cohesion) aims to increase Pcoh(a_use) when N_T > 0, yet Table 1 shows lower compositional complexity under Boids. This undermines the claim that cohesion fosters collaborative tool use in the current implementation and should be reconciled either by revising the implementation or by adjusting incentives.

18.text: Equation (2) (separation tiers) and Equation (5) (alignment boost) are clear but are only instantiated as prompt text fragments. Because the orchestrator “deterministically proceeds to a build action each round” (Section 3.2), these preference functions are not part of a decision policy; they are narrative guidance. This discrepancy between formalism and implementation should be highlighted and empirically evaluated via ablations.

0.text: The paper does not evaluate, analyze, or even motivate the method in NLP contexts. There is no experiment on language models, text classification, sequence tagging, MT, or any NLP-relevant optimization regime. As written, this is an ML/optimizers proof-of-concept, not an ACL paper.

1.text: Experiments are confined to 10D analytic functions and a small synthetic linear regression. No neural training, no stochastic minibatching, and no high-dimensional tasks typical of NLP optimization.

2.text: Table 1 contains repeated, identical final losses across methods and settings that are implausible and call into question the evaluation: For Rastrigin, many entries for SGD, Momentum, and Evolved are exactly 37.81 across budgets and dimensions (e.g., 10D/200, 10D/300, 10D/400, 20D/200, 20D/300, 20D/400), and multiple methods tie exactly. This strongly suggests a metric saturation, clipping artifact, or bug in logging/evaluation. The same pattern appears with 65.67 in 20D. This must be investigated, clarified, and fixed if it is a tooling artifact. On Ackley, several results differ only at the second decimal place with small, overlapping variation, making it hard to substantiate claims of competitiveness beyond noise. Although Appendix B adds error bands, the main text’s Table 1 patterns remain suspicious.

3.text: The paper claims generalization beyond the training landscape, but Figure 3 (middle) described as a “Pareto cloud” appears to show a single marker rather than a cloud of elites; this contradicts the narrative about rich trade-offs across rules. If the figure is representative, it undermines the generalization/portfolio claim; if not, the figure is misleading and needs correction.

4.text: The transfer experiment (Figure 2) is a single small linear regression task. It does not reflect optimization challenges in modern NLP models, where adaptive methods and schedules are critical. The evidence does not support broader generalization claims.

5.text: The DSL (Eq. 1–3) closely matches the Adam-family structure with discrete token grids for coefficients and exponents. While the end-to-end autonomy is emphasized, the optimizer search space and evolutionary loop are conventional; comparisons against prior symbolic optimizer search or genetic programming baselines are not provided.

6.text: The mutation strategy is very simple (token flips). There is no analysis of search efficiency, diversity maintenance, or overfitting to evaluation protocols.

7.text: Baseline tuning is unclear. For Adam/Momentum, hyperparameter choices can drastically alter behavior. The DSL discretization forces narrow choices; it is possible that the “evolved” rules merely pick slightly better learning rates or omit normalization, which can be replicated by hand-tuned baselines. Provide fair tuning for all baselines with ranges comparable to the evolved rules’ ranges.

8.text: Section 4.6 claims ablations “reveal performance degradations,” yet quantitative ablation tables are not shown in the main text. The qualitative Figure 4 shows similar convergence across top-5 rules, but causal attribution to specific tokens would benefit from a more systematic ablation table.

9.text: Stability is enforced by clipping and NaN guards (Section 3.2, 3.4), potentially masking pathological behaviors. Without reporting how often guards trigger, it is hard to assess whether rules are inherently robust. This is particularly important if transferring to noisy, high-dimensional NLP training.

10.text: The manuscript centers the “AI-authored” process. While interesting, it does not compensate for the lack of strong empirical validation. For acceptance at a selective venue, the technical contribution should stand on its own merits; here, it remains exploratory.

11.text: Figure 1 right (Ackley) shows all methods improving slowly with small separations and overlapping bands (Appendix Figure 6), so the text’s statement “competitive on Ackley” needs nuance; the evolved rule is not clearly better.

12.text: Figure 3 right (token frequency dynamics) is potentially insightful, but the text asserts “preference for p=0 normalization and moderate β_v” without quantifying how these choices affected outcomes across tasks. A clearer mapping from color scale to token prevalence and its correlation with performance is needed.

13.text: Table 2 presents top-5 evolved rules that largely look like SGD variants with partial momentum and v-tracking but no normalization. Without showing a setting where these surpass tuned Momentum or AdamW on realistic tasks (e.g., small CNN or transformer finetuning), the “library” seems of limited practical significance.

14.text: While the appendix lists JSON artifacts and an anonymized repo, the main paper does not fully specify exact Adam variant details (e.g., bias correction, ε placement), nor whether weight decay or AdamW were considered. 0.text: Both benchmarks are small (100 Chinese idioms, 100 English words) and rendered in what appears to be a single font and resolution (Section 3.2). The paper sometimes generalizes to “universal failure mode” and “cross-script blind spot” (Abstract, Section 5) that the presented evidence does not fully justify. More languages, fonts, sizes, background clutter, and parameterized overlap/offsets are needed to substantiate universality.

1.text: Section 3.4 mentions 10 participants and “report aggregate accuracy with confidence intervals,” but tables and figures present only point values “100%.” There are no CIs or per-item confusion matrices shown. If accuracy is truly 100%, it should be shown transparently, and any borderline items should be discussed. Without basic details (participant demographics, display conditions, timing, screening), the human–model gap is hard to calibrate.

2.text: API inference temperature, sampling parameters, and retry policies are not specified. Several results depend on prompts (Tables 1–2), but the number of generations per item per prompt is unclear; Section 7 of the checklist mentions “averaged over 2 runs,” which is weak given high variance in API responses. Stronger aggregation (n≥5–10 samples per item) or deterministic decoding would yield more defensible estimates.

3.text: The benchmark targets reading robustness. However, there are no comparisons to OCR-specific systems (e.g., Tesseract, TrOCR, CRNN/CTC variants) or to simple classical segmentation pipelines (color-thresholding and layer separation in the English overlap; connected-component analysis or radical-level segmentation for Chinese). Such baselines would help determine whether the deficit is specific to current VLM architectures or a broader vision issue. As it stands, the conclusion that “architectural blind spot” is the main cause is plausible but not isolated from simpler explanations.

4.text: The psychophysics framing (Section 2.3) suggests controlled variation. Yet the paper uses a single fusion strength per stimulus. There are no curves showing recognition as a function of overlap amount, color contrast, stroke collision density, or cut axis/offset. This prevents understanding where models fail and what design choices matter, and it weakens the claim that the effect is systematic rather than stimulus-specific.

5.text: For idioms, a difflib-based “Average Similarity” is reported (Section 3.4, Table 3). This string similarity can be misleading for Chinese, where a single wrong character often changes meaning entirely. Edit distance or character-level accuracy distributions would be more interpretable. Also, the preprocessing “removing all non-Chinese characters using regex” could inadvertently bias results if models output near-miss characters or include punctuation; details on normalization and mapping variants are missing.

6.text: The paper asserts that models produce “unrelated or incoherent outputs” (Abstract, Section 4.1) but provides no systematic error taxonomy or examples. Qualitative panels contrasting human-readable composites with typical model outputs would substantiate this claim and guide future mitigation.

7.text: Figure 5 and Figure 6 list hardest/easiest cases, but the methodology for ranking, number of trials per item, and model aggregation are unclear. In Figure 5, several “easiest” words still top out below 60% accuracy, which suggests limited signal and small-N effects rather than clean separability. The text states humans show “no meaningful difference” across these items, but no human-item-level stats are shown.

0.text: Precision is defined as the percentage of “positive” sentences, but negative sentences are created by LLaMA2-70B via edits and word shuffling. The paper states “a negative sentence does not necessarily indicate complete irrelevance,” suggesting partial correctness remains. Without a rigorous annotation protocol quantifying actual factual correctness per token/entity, the precision axis is noisy. This undermines the central causal narrative. Please clarify exactly how many incorrect propositions per negative sentence are typical and how that was verified beyond heuristic generation.

1.text: Recall is proxied by the number of subcaptions (0–3), but the study does not show that adding subcaptions monotonically increases factual coverage of unique entities or attributes in the whole image. Table 1 lists average nouns and tokens per condition, but not unique grounded facts. More content length is not necessarily higher recall.

2.text: Table 1 shows substantial growth in average tokens with more submasks (e.g., 54.8 → 157.8) and more nouns. This simultaneously changes length, density, and topical breadth, so the recall axis is entangled with several factors. No controls exist for fixed-length variants, which makes it hard to attribute gains to recall rather than length or language modeling benefits.

3.text: The human-annotated analysis uses 8,012 images. Fine-tuning PixArt-α with LoRA for 10 epochs on such a small corpus might produce idiosyncratic effects. The paper claims broad implications for T2I training, but does not test on larger or more diverse human-captioned datasets, nor provide variance across seeds. This weakens generality.

4.text: The compositional evaluation pipeline relies heavily on BLIP2, CLIP, and object detectors as task-specific judges, which may share biases with training encoders. There is no human evaluation to confirm that the reported differences reflect actual image–text faithfulness rather than judge-specific artifacts.

5.text: Section 4 uses a modified FaithScore with GPT-3.5 for decomposition and LLaVA1.5-13B as the final judge. Since LLaVA is also one of the caption generators, the evaluation likely favors it, as the authors note in Limitations. However, this bias is not quantified, and the probe uses only 1,000 samples from 118k. Table 4’s differences could be within noise if not statistically tested.

6.text: The revised decomposition (ENTITY, SHAPE, COLOR, TEXTURE, SPATIAL, NON-SPATIAL) is reasonable, but the paper does not release prompts, system templates, or adjudication rubrics, leaving reproducibility uncertain.

7.text: Human-caption analysis fine-tunes PixArt-α on Dense Caption Dataset-derived captions, then evaluates on T2I-CompBench. The synthetic-caption study trains on MS-COCO and again evaluates on T2I-CompBench. The different training corpora and different T2I backbones (PixArt-α vs SD2.1/SDXL) introduce confounds. While the qualitative trend is similar, it is difficult to separate effects of model family, dataset domain, and caption regime.

8.text: No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported for Tables 2–3. Some deltas are small, especially at higher precision levels where recall adds marginal gains. Without error bars, it is hard to tell whether improvements are robust.

9.text: LoRA rank, text encoder freeze policy, effective training tokens, and sampling details are missing for PixArt-α. For SD2.1 and SDXL, the paper states 100k iterations, batch size 8, LR 1e-4, but not validation protocols, prompt sampling, checkpoint selection strategy, or the total compute. No ablation checks if longer training equalizes differences between captioners.

10.text: The diffusion loss is given, but the text encoder τθ(c) and image encoder ε(x) are only briefly mentioned and not described for the specific backbones used in each experiment. Since the analysis centers on text conditioning, more precision about which encoders are trained or frozen in each setting would help interpretability.

11.text: Figure 1 suggests a larger gradient along the precision axis than along the submask axis, matching the narrative. However, the figure’s color scale and absolute ranges are not explicitly tied to the task-average scores in Table 2, which might confuse readers trying to map visual to numeric gains.

12.text: Table 2 supports the claim that at 0% precision, increasing submasks from 0 to 3 yields a nontrivial average increase (0.2377 → 0.3000). At 100% precision, 0 to 3 submasks improves from 0.3196 → 0.3471, a smaller margin, consistent with diminishing returns from recall. Nevertheless, the paper does not quantify effect sizes or relative improvements per category; some cells show very small shifts that may be within expected variance.

13.text: Table 3 indicates that LLaVA captions outperform others in average scores on both SD2.1 and SDXL. However, because Table 4 reveals heterogeneity in entity count and faithscore, it would help to correlate those metrics explicitly with Table 3 performance via regression or controlled subsampling to strengthen the causal reading of “precision dominates recall.”

For precision, provide human spot-checks quantifying the number and type of incorrect propositions per negative sentence. For recall, report unique grounded entities/attributes covered by subcaptions using a VQA or grounding tool, rather than relying on token/noun counts.

0.text: While the SCM in Figure 4 and Equation (1) motivate intervening on context X, the actual intervention is implemented as stochastic perturbations to output distributions, not as an interventional mechanism on inputs or representations. The paper does not establish that adding Gumbel noise to p(y|q,v,s,a) is a valid surrogate for do(X=x̂) in the stated SCM, beyond intuition. This weakens the causal justification and risks over-claiming “counterfactual” benefits.

1.text: The primary debiasing baseline is VDD adapted from images to videos. Other strong test-time or light-weight training methods are not compared, such as non-contrastive activation steering or alternative prior/posterior calibration schemes. Without stronger baselines, it is hard to isolate whether DCVC’s advantage is from better modeling or simply from introducing a small supervised head.

2.text: Results are reported on development splits for Social-IQ-2.0 and DeSIQ-2.0 (Table 1) rather than dedicated test sets. This complicates judging generalization and raises the chance of selection bias in hyperparameter tuning. Also, the explanation for very high LMM accuracy on DeSIQ-2.0 is plausible but anecdotal; more rigorous analysis of option semantics and dataset artifacts would strengthen the claim.

3.text: Section 3.4 provides the noise distributions and high-level FlipDA filtering, but key thresholds and selection criteria are under-specified. For instance, the paper states “select augmented samples with the highest probabilities for flipped labels,” but does not detail percentile thresholds, proportion kept per instance, or whether class balance across flips is controlled. This leaves reproducibility gaps and makes it hard to reason about why VCDA helps in Figure 5 beyond general augmentation effects.

4.text: The core DC input is Concat(hq ∘ p(y|q,v,s,a), hq ∘ p(y|q)) in Equation (2). However, there is no probe or ablation that replaces p(y|q) with other priors (e.g., frequency-based priors from training labels, or priors estimated from a different LLM) to test whether the method is specifically mitigating language priors from the same LMM, or simply learning to trust whichever prior correlates with labels. Table 2 drops the MSE and VCDA, but does not isolate alternative priors.

5.text: Figure 2: The bar/line plot shows mean probabilities for emotions across input settings. The blue/orange/yellow bars for W/O V,S, V, and V+S are close, which visually underpins the claim that language-driven outputs dominate. However, the figure would be stronger if accompanied by statistical tests quantifying the similarity between “with” and “without” context distributions.

6.text: Figure 3: The pipeline makes clear that VCDA perturbs p(y|·) rather than inputs and that a learned DC calibrates the outputs. This clarity is a strength, but it also highlights that the “counterfactual” claim is at the output layer, not at the causal variable X, which exacerbates Weakness 1.

7.text: Figure 5: The bar chart shows VCDA’s additional gains are largest at 30% data. This is useful, but a line plot with error bars over multiple random seeds would make the conclusion more robust.

8.text: Table 1: DCVC yields substantially higher accuracy than both baselines and VDD. However, the comparison includes a fine-tuned CREMA number, which is not a like-for-like zero-shot baseline. A stronger comparison would also include fine-tuning with ordinary augmentations versus with VCDA.

9.text: Table 2: The ablation shows each component helps, yet the absolute drops are modest between -VCDA and -MSE Loss. Reporting confidence intervals or multiple runs would help judge stability.

10.text: Table 3: Gumbel noise slightly outperforms Logistic and Gaussian, but the differences are small; again, no variance estimates are provided, so the strength of the conclusion is uncertain.

11.text: Kim et al., “What if...?: Counterfactual Inception to Mitigate Hallucination Effects in Large Multimodal Models,” 2024 — Proposes counterfactual cues and dual-modality verification to reduce hallucinations in LMMs; directly related to the paper’s counterfactual framing. Should be discussed in Section 2 and compared as an alternative test-time intervention in Section 5.1.

12.text: Howard et al., “Uncovering Bias in Large Vision-Language Models at Scale with Counterfactuals,” 2025 — Large-scale counterfactual evaluation of social bias in VLMs; relevant to metrics and broader evaluation design. Should be cited in Related Work and discussed in Section 5 as guidance for more systematic bias measurement.

13.text: Ratzlaff et al., “Debias your Large Multi-Modal Model at Test-Time with Non-Contrastive Visual Attribute Steering,” 2025 — A training-free representation steering approach to mitigate demographic bias; serves as a competitive baseline for test-time debiasing. Add to Section 2 and include as a baseline where feasible.

14.text: Zhang et al., “CounterCurate: Enhancing Physical and Semantic Visio-Linguistic Compositional Reasoning via Counterfactual Examples,” 2024 — Uses curated counterfactual examples for robustness; closely related to the paper’s VCDA idea. Discuss in Section 3.4 and contrast curated vs. virtual counterfactuals.

15.text: Vo et al., “Vision Language Models are Biased,” 2026 — Introduces VLMBias benchmark and counterfactual manipulations for simple counting tasks; relevant as a standardized bias benchmark. Discuss in Related Work and consider as an additional evaluation in future versions.

16.text: Jin et al., “MMToM-QA: Multimodal Theory of Mind Question Answering,” 2024 — A socially grounded QA benchmark. Add in Section 4.1 as a relevant dataset to test whether language-bias mitigation aids deeper social reasoning.

17.text: Ryan et al., “Humor in Pixels: Benchmarking Large Multimodal Models Understanding of Online Comics,” 2025 — A socially nuanced, multimodal understanding benchmark. Mention in Related Work and consider as an orthogonal testbed for generalization of DCVC.

18.text: Liang et al., “Envision, Attend, Then Respond: Counterfactual Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision-Language Models,” 2026 — Training-free counterfactual mitigation evaluated on VLMBias and POPE; relevant to the paper’s counterfactual narrative and suitable as a stronger baseline. Discuss in Section 2 and, if feasible, compare experimentally.

19.text: Strengthen the causal story: Provide a clearer theoretical connection between do(X) in Equation (1) and the practical VCDA perturbations to p(y|·). For example, show that controlled perturbations to specific modalities produce predictable shifts in p(y|·) that align with the SCM, or introduce a representation-level intervention that more closely approximates do(X=x̂).

20.text: Expand baselines: Include at least one additional competitive test-time debiasing method beyond VDD, such as representation steering or alternative calibration schemes. Also compare to a small learned post-hoc classifier trained on features without VCDA to test whether gains stem from augmentations or simply from supervision.

21.text: Report test results and variance: If test splits are available, include them. For Tables 1–3, report mean and standard deviation over multiple runs or bootstrap intervals to assess statistical significance.

22.text: VCDA details and diagnostics: Specify selection thresholds, proportions of flips kept, degree of perturbation versus flip rate, and whether label distributions remain balanced. Add an analysis that relates perturbation magnitude to flip quality and final accuracy.

23.text: Probing priors: Replace p(y|q) with alternative priors (e.g., from a different LLM or a frequency-based prior) to test the calibration network’s specific sensitivity to language priors. An ablation that removes p(y|q) but keeps the same parameter count would also isolate its contribution.
